analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans legally buy up to a 90-day supply of cheaper prescription drugs from licensed Canadian pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The drug-importation bill died in committee: it was introduced in July 2002 with 4 cosponsors, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let individuals legally import up to a 90-day supply of prescription drugs from registered Canadian pharmacies, where the same medicines often cost much less than in the United States. It would also require online drug sellers to disclose who they are and who their pharmacists are, and bar internet prescriptions without a real in-person doctor visit. The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress adjourned.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. prices for prescription drugs, especially older adults on fixed incomes, would be able to import up to a 90-day supply of their medications from licensed Canadian pharmacies, where the same drugs often sell for far less. Patients buying drugs online would get clearer information about who is selling and who is prescribing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans paying high US prescription prices

how_it_helps.text: Permits individuals to import up to a 90-day personal supply of FDA-approved prescription drugs from registered, licensed Canadian pharmacies with a valid U.S. prescription, where prices are typically far lower.

Requires HHS to study the authenticity and quality of imported drugs, and to tighten or end the waiver if a significant public health threat emerges; it could also extend the waiver to other countries if none is found.
Requires internet drug sellers to display their business identity, their pharmacists' names, and the states where they are licensed to dispense, so buyers can verify who they are dealing with.

Bars internet sellers from arranging prescriptions when the prescribing doctor never saw the patient in person, closing a loophole used by rogue online pharmacies, and lets state attorneys general sue to enforce the rules.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would lose sales as Americans buy lower-priced Canadian versions of the same drugs. Online drug sellers would also face new disclosure rules and a ban on prescribing without an in-person doctor visit, and the bill would tighten limits on importing controlled substances without a prescription.

drawbacks.text: Personal drug importation carries safety risks: the bill itself concedes the point by requiring a one-year government study of the quality and authenticity of imported drugs and letting the Secretary terminate the waiver if a significant public health threat is found.

The safety study is effectively a tripwire: if the Secretary of HHS concludes imports threaten public health, the whole importation provision can be ended by a notice in the Federal Register, so the access it promises is never guaranteed.
The bill shrinks the amount of controlled substances a person may import without a prescription from 50 dosage units to 10, a restriction for people bringing back their own medication from abroad.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients is real and direct: the same FDA-approved drugs often cost far less in Canada, and legalizing personal importation would immediately put that price gap within reach of people who today pay U.S. prices. The costs are modest and the bill manages them itself, with registration of pharmacies, quantity limits, a quality study, and a safety off-switch. The bigger question is scale: personal importation is a workaround that helps individuals but does not fix why U.S. drug prices are higher, and the bill's outcome hinged on a Secretary's judgment about safety.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last months of the session, sent to a House committee and then its health subcommittee, and sat there with no action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 25, 2002, with four Democratic cosponsors, and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Four days later it was sent to the Subcommittee on Health, where no further action was taken.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, with the bill still in committee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, who kept U.S. prices for their drugs intact because cheaper Canadian imports were never authorized. Americans paying U.S. drug prices gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept higher US prices

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the four cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Tom Allen, Marion Berry, Frank Pallone, and Ted Strickland

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: House Committee on Energy and Commerce and its Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: The committee and its health subcommittee took no action on the bill after it was referred, and no markup or floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended.

against.name: Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee to which the bill was referred, never scheduled it for consideration; committee leaders of both parties generally resisted drug importation bills that brand-name manufacturers opposed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all four cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled House never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would open a legal channel for Americans to buy the same drugs at lower Canadian prices, cutting into U.S. sales. Because the bill died in committee, the industry kept its higher U.S. prices untouched.

Online sellers would face new disclosure requirements and a ban on issuing prescriptions without an in-person medical evaluation, which would shut out sketchy operators. Legitimate internet pharmacies could also gain if personal importation became legal.

Registered Canadian pharmacies could sell to U.S. patients under the waiver, but only for personal use in limited quantities, and the Secretary could terminate the arrangement if the safety study found a public health threat.
